query: For high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer that provides oxidation resistance? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison that would reveal it, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys that include elements such as Cr and Ta, deliberately reducing the concentration of less-protective components (e.g., Ti) and promoting a refined microstructure leads to a preferential outward diffusion of Cr and Ta at high temperature. This in turn supports the in situ formation and long‐term retention of a dense, continuous CrTaO4‐based oxide layer that acts as an effective barrier to oxygen ingress, thus enhancing the oxidation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi-principal element refractory high-entropy alloy containing Cr, Ta, and lower Ti content, processed to obtain an ultrafine or highly homogeneous microstructure.
generation.intervention: Alter the alloy chemistry (reduce Ti and/or other rapidly diffusing elements) and apply a processing route (e.g., friction processing) to refine the grain structure.
generation.conditions: High-temperature oxidation in air (e.g., exposure at 1100 °C for extended durations, such as 100–200 hours).
generation.structural_mediator: A fine-grained (ultrafine) microstructure that, via enhanced grain boundary density, promotes uniform cation diffusion and local enrichment of Cr and Ta at the surface.
generation.mechanism: Due to differences in diffusivities and oxidation activation energies, Cr and Ta diffuse outward more slowly but accumulate at the surface. This selective enrichment, coupled with the slowed diffusion inherent to high-entropy systems, yields the nucleation and growth of a protective CrTaO4-based oxide. The resulting continuous, adherent oxide scale impedes further oxygen transport into the bulk alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline alloy with higher Ti content and coarse microstructure, the processed alloy will exhibit a significantly lower oxidation rate (lower mass gain per unit area) with a continuous, adherent oxide scale predominantly comprised of CrTaO4.
generation.baseline: High-entropy alloy samples with higher levels of Ti (or other fast-diffusing, less protective elements) and/or coarse grain structures, which tend to form heterogeneous, spall-prone oxide layers leading to higher mass gains during oxidation.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for refractory or high-temperature high-entropy alloys exposed in oxidative atmospheres above approximately 1000 °C. At lower temperatures or in different alloy systems where other oxide species dominate (e.g., primarily alumina or chromia layers), the mechanism may differ.
generation.uncertainty: While evidence from NV1 alloy studies (PMC6513993::web::015::discussion) and oxidation kinetics in ultrafine-grained AlCoCrFeNi alloys (PMC9026100::web::017::oxidation_kinetics) support the beneficial role of controlled element diffusion and microstructural refinement, the exact interplay between CrTaO4 formation and the potential formation of secondary oxide phases (such as Al2O3 and Cr2O3) remains uncertain. Additional kinetic measurements are required to fully resolve these interactions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples: one set with reduced Ti content and an ultrafine-grained microstructure (via high-strain processing) and a control set with conventional Ti content and coarse grains. Expose both sample sets to high-temperature oxidation (e.g., 1100 °C in air) for 200 hours.
measurements: Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) to record mass gain kinetics over time
Surface and cross-sectional phase analysis using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) to quantify the composition and continuity of the oxide layer
Microscopy (SEM/TEM) to assess oxide scale morphology and adhesion
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy with reduced Ti content and refined microstructure does not show a significantly lower mass gain rate, nor the formation of a continuous, adherent CrTaO4-based oxide layer compared to the control sample, the hypothesis will be falsified.
